titulo_es: False friends between English and Spanish
descripcion_es: Words that look like Spanish words but mean something different.
resumen: English words that look like a Spanish word but mean something else (actually, sensible, library). They are a constant source of mistakes, even at advanced levels.

explicacion.texto: The table gives the false friend, what it really means and how to say in English the Spanish word it looks like.

cabecera: To say the Spanish word, use…
filas: in the end, finally (es: al final, finalmente)
a place where you borrow books (es: biblioteca)
to be present at (es: asistir a)
atender → to deal with, to serve
to act as if something is true (es: fingir)
to become aware of (es: darse cuenta)
to start again after a pause (es: reanudar)
to challenge, to dispute (es: impugnar, disputar)
a conversation, a debate (not hostile) (es: conversación, debate)
a victim, an injured person (es: víctima, herido)
a person who directs an orchestra; a ticket inspector (es: director de orquesta, revisor)
unable to empty the bowels easily (es: estreñido)
a substance that keeps food fresh (es: conservante)
an opinion about what someone should do (es: consejo)
a place with tents or huts (es: campamento)
a register, a disc, a best result (es: registro, disco, marca)
a working life, a profession (es: carrera profesional)

items: Some are only partly false friends: “compromise” is “an agreement with concessions”, not Spanish “compromiso” in the sense of “commitment”.
“Argument” is a quarrel or row, but also a logical argument.

ejemplos.frase: I thought he was Italian, but he's actually from Argentina.
ejemplos.traduccion: Creía que era italiano, pero en realidad es de Argentina.

ejemplos.frase: It would be sensible to book the hotel in advance.
ejemplos.traduccion: Sería sensato reservar el hotel con antelación.

ejemplos.frase: She was so embarrassed that she turned red.
ejemplos.traduccion: Le dio tanta vergüenza que se puso roja.

ejemplos.frase: I suddenly realised I had left my keys at home.
ejemplos.traduccion: De repente me di cuenta de que me había dejado las llaves en casa.

ejemplos.frase: Talks will resume after the summer break.
ejemplos.traduccion: Las conversaciones se reanudarán después del parón de verano.

ejemplos.frase: Hundreds of people attended the funeral.
ejemplos.traduccion: Cientos de personas asistieron al funeral.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: My sister is embarrassed; the baby is due in May.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: My sister is pregnant; the baby is due in May.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I can't support this noise any longer.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I can't stand this noise any longer.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: To put up with something annoying (es: soportar) is “stand” or “bear”.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Can you resume the article in three lines?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Can you summarise the article in three lines?
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “resumir” is “summarise”; “resume” means to start again (es: reanudar).

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: He is very sympathetic; everybody likes him.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He is very nice; everybody likes him.

ejercicios.frase: I bought three novels at the library on the corner.
respuestas: I bought three novels at the bookshop on the corner.
I bought three novels at the bookstore on the corner.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table on the card shows that library is a place where you borrow books (es: biblioteca) and that a shop that sells books (es: librería) is a bookshop (British) or bookstore (American). The clue in this sentence is the verb bought: in a library you borrow books, you don't buy them. So library must be replaced by bookshop or bookstore; both versions are correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Where you buy books is a “bookshop / bookstore”; a “library” is where you borrow them (es: biblioteca).
ejercicios.traduccion: Compré tres novelas en la librería de la esquina.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I bought three novels at the library on the corner.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: a library is where you borrow books, not where you buy them.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I bought three novels at the bookshelf on the corner.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A bookshelf is a piece of furniture for books, not a shop.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I bought three novels at the librery on the corner.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Apart from being a typo, it is still the false friend; the shop is a bookshop or bookstore.

glosario.definicion_l: a room where books are kept · a collection of literary documents or records kept for reference or borrowing
original and of a kind not seen before · pleasantly new or different

ejercicios.frase: More than 200 people assisted the conference.
respuestas: More than 200 people attended the conference.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that to assist means “to help” and that “asistir a un acto” (to be present at an event) is to attend. The clue is the object the conference and the number of people: it is about being present, not about helping. Attend is transitive, so it takes no preposition: attended the conference, without to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To be present at an event (es: asistir a) is “attend”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Más de 200 personas asistieron a la conferencia.

errores_previstos.respuesta: More than 200 people assisted the conference.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: assist means to help, not to be present.

errores_previstos.respuesta: More than 200 people attended to the conference.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Attend to means “to deal with, to look after”; for being present at an event, attend takes no preposition.

errores_previstos.respuesta: More than 200 people assisted to the conference.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A word-for-word copy of Spanish “asistieron a”; the correct verb is attend, without to.

ejercicios.frase: He ___ to be ill so he could miss the exam.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives to pretend as “to act as if something is true” (es: fingir), while Spanish “pretender” is to intend or to aim. The clue is the purpose so he could miss the exam: acting ill so as not to go is pretending. Pretend to be ill means exactly that (es: fingir estar enfermo).
ejercicios.traduccion: Fingió estar enfermo para poder faltar al examen.

por_opcion.pretended: Correct: pretend = act as if (es: fingir); pretended to be ill = acted as if he were ill.
por_opcion.intended: Incorrect: intend means “to plan to” (es: tener la intención de, pretender); intended to be ill makes no sense here.
por_opcion.realised: Incorrect: realise means “to become aware” (es: darse cuenta), not “to carry out” or “to pretend”.
por_opcion.assisted: Incorrect: assist means “to help” and is not followed by to be.

ejercicios.frase: The new film was a huge ___: it broke box office records.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that exit means “way out” (es: salida) and that Spanish “éxito” is success. The clue is the explanation after the colon: breaking box-office records is a triumph. Success is the noun; succession and successor look similar but mean something else.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “éxito” is “success”; “exit” is the way out (es: salida).
ejercicios.traduccion: La nueva película fue un éxito enorme: batió récords de taquilla.

por_opcion.success: Correct: success = a good result, a triumph (es: éxito).
por_opcion.exit: Incorrect: exit is “the way out” (emergency exit); it is the false friend of Spanish “éxito”.
por_opcion.succession: Incorrect: succession is a series, or taking over a position (es: sucesión).
por_opcion.successor: Incorrect: successor is the person who follows another (es: sucesor).

glosario.definicion_l: an event that accomplishes its intended purpose · an attainment that is successful
an opening that permits escape or release · euphemistic expressions for death
total admission receipts for an entertainment · the office where tickets of admission are sold

ejercicios.frase: My skin is very ___ to the sun, so I always wear sunscreen.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that English sensible means “showing good judgement” (es: sensato) and that Spanish “sensible” is sensitive. The clue is the skin and the sun: it is about reacting easily to a stimulus, which is the meaning of sensitive. Also, sensitive is followed by to (sensitive to the sun).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “sensible” is “sensitive”; English “sensible” means showing good judgement (es: sensato).
ejercicios.traduccion: Tengo la piel muy sensible al sol, así que siempre me pongo protector solar.

por_opcion.sensitive: Correct: sensitive = reacting easily to something (es: sensible).
por_opcion.sensible: Incorrect: English sensible means “showing good judgement” (es: sensato) (a sensible decision).
por_opcion.sensory: Incorrect: sensory means “related to the senses” (es: sensorial) (sensory organs).
por_opcion.sensual: Incorrect: sensual means related to physical pleasure (es: sensual).

glosario.definicion_l: responsive to physical stimuli · being susceptible to the attitudes, feelings, or circumstances of others
showing reason or sound judgment · able to feel or perceive
a cream spread on the skin; contains a chemical (as PABA) to filter out ultraviolet light and so protect from sunburn

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (to become aware), in the past.
ejercicios.frase: When I got to the station, I ___ I had forgotten my ticket.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives to realise as “to become aware” (es: darse cuenta), while Spanish “realizar” is to carry out. The clue is the sentence that follows (I had forgotten my ticket): it is a sudden discovery. Both the British spelling realised and the American realized are accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cuando llegué a la estación, me di cuenta de que me había olvidado el billete.

errores_previstos.respuesta: noticed of
errores_previstos.explicacion: A word-for-word copy of Spanish “darse cuenta de”; notice takes no of, and the instruction asks for one word: realised.

errores_previstos.respuesta: realise
errores_previstos.explicacion: The instruction asks for the past: realised.

errores_previstos.respuesta: knew
errores_previstos.explicacion: Knew means you already had the information; it does not express the moment of becoming aware, which is realised.

ejercicios.frase: Actually, the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
respuestas: Currently, the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
At present, the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
Now the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that actually means “in fact” (es: en realidad) and that Spanish “actualmente” is currently or at present. The clue is the contrast in time with last year: the present moment is contrasted with last year, which is the meaning of “actualmente”. Currently, at present and now are accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Actualmente, la empresa tiene 300 empleados, pero el año pasado tenía 500.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Actually, the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: actually means “in fact”, not “at present”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Actualy, the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Apart from the typo, it is still the false friend; say currently or at present.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In actuality, the company employs 300 people, but last year it had 500.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In actuality means “in fact”, like actually; it does not express the present moment.

glosario.definicion_l: in actual fact · used to imply that one would expect the fact to be the opposite of that stated; surprisingly

ejercicios.frase: The two neighbours had a terrible ___ about the noise.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that discussion is a conversation or debate that is not hostile, and that a “discusión” in the sense of a quarrel is an argument. The clue is the adjective terrible and the cause (noise between neighbours): it is an angry quarrel. That is why only argument fits; have an argument is the usual collocation.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los dos vecinos tuvieron una discusión terrible por el ruido.

por_opcion.argument: Correct: argument = a heated discussion, a verbal fight.
por_opcion.discussion: Incorrect: discussion is a calm exchange of ideas (a discussion about the budget); it does not convey anger.
por_opcion.debate: Incorrect: debate is an organised or public debate, not a quarrel between neighbours.

glosario.definicion_l: a fact or assertion offered as evidence that something is true · a contentious speech act; a dispute where there is strong disagreement
an extended communication (often interactive) dealing with some particular topic · an exchange of views on some topic
a person who lives (or is located) near another · a nearby object of the same kind

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (to start again).
ejercicios.frase: The match will ___ as soon as the rain stops.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives to resume as “to start again after a pause” (es: reanudar) (and warns that Spanish “resumir” is to summarise). The clue is as soon as the rain stops: the match has been interrupted and will start again. Restart and continue are also accepted; they express the same idea less formally.
ejercicios.traduccion: El partido se reanudará en cuanto deje de llover.

errores_previstos.respuesta: summarise
errores_previstos.explicacion: Summarise means to give a short version (es: resumir); here it is about starting again: resume.

errores_previstos.respuesta: renew
errores_previstos.explicacion: Renew means to extend (a contract, a passport) (es: renovar), not to start again.

errores_previstos.respuesta: resumes
errores_previstos.explicacion: After will the verb goes in the infinitive without -s: resume.

ejercicios.frase: I'm constipated: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
respuestas: I've got a cold: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
I have a cold: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
I've caught a cold: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that constipated means unable to empty the bowels easily (es: estreñido) and that Spanish “estar constipado” is to have a cold. The clue is the symptoms (sneezing, my nose is running), which are those of a cold. Have a cold, have got a cold and have caught a cold are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “estar constipado” is “have a cold”; “constipated” means something else (es: estreñido).
ejercicios.traduccion: Estoy constipado: no paro de estornudar y me moquea la nariz.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm constipated: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: constipated does not mean having a cold (es: estreñido).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm cold: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
errores_previstos.explicacion: I'm cold means you feel the low temperature (es: tengo frío); the illness is I have a cold.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have cold: I keep sneezing and my nose is running.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The article is missing: have a cold.

glosario.definicion_l: impede with a clog or as if with a clog · cause to be constipated

ejercicios.frase: Put all the invoices in the blue ___ on my desk.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that carpet is a floor covering (es: alfombra, moqueta) and that Spanish “carpeta” is folder. The clue is the contents (the invoices) and the place (the desk): you need something to keep papers in. Folder is the word; a briefcase is for carrying documents, but it is a bag.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “carpeta” is “folder”; a “carpet” covers the floor (es: alfombra).
ejercicios.traduccion: Mete todas las facturas en la carpeta azul que hay en mi mesa.

por_opcion.folder: Correct: folder = a cover for keeping papers (es: carpeta).
por_opcion.carpet: Incorrect: carpet is a floor covering (es: alfombra, moqueta); it is the false friend of Spanish “carpeta”.
por_opcion.briefcase: Incorrect: a briefcase is a bag for documents (es: maletín); you could put papers in it, but it is not a folder and is not usually kept “on my desk” for filing.

glosario.definicion_l: a small book usually having a paper cover · covering that is folded over to protect the contents
floor covering consisting of a piece of thick heavy fabric (usually with nap or pile) · a natural object that resembles or suggests a carpet
an itemized statement of money owed for goods shipped or services rendered · send a bill to
a case with a handle; for carrying papers or files or books

ejercicios.frase: It was pure ___ that we met in Rome.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that casualty means a victim or an injured person (es: víctima, herido) and that Spanish “casualidad” is chance or coincidence. The clue is the expression pure ___: a meeting by accident. Pure chance is the usual collocation (es: pura casualidad).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “casualidad” is “chance” or “coincidence”; a “casualty” is a victim.
ejercicios.traduccion: Fue pura casualidad que nos conociéramos en Roma.

por_opcion.chance: Correct: chance = luck, accident (es: casualidad, azar); pure chance (es: pura casualidad).
por_opcion.casualty: Incorrect: a casualty is a victim or an injured person (in an accident or a war).
por_opcion.casualness: Incorrect: casualness means “a relaxed, informal attitude”, not chance.

glosario.definicion_l: occurring or appearing or singled out by chance · a possibility due to a favorable combination of circumstances
someone injured or killed or captured or missing in a military engagement · someone injured or killed in an accident
an event that might have been arranged although it was really accidental · the quality of occupying the same position or area in space

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (showing good judgement).
ejercicios.frase: Saving part of your salary every month is a very ___ idea.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that English sensible means “showing good judgement” (es: sensato). The clue is the idea itself (saving every month), which is prudent and reasonable. It is the reverse of exercise 5: here sensible is used because the meaning is “showing good judgement”. Wise and good are also accepted; they express a similar opinion.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ahorrar una parte del sueldo cada mes es una idea muy sensata.

errores_previstos.respuesta: sensitive
errores_previstos.explicacion: Sensitive means easily affected, delicate (es: sensible); an idea showing good judgement is sensible.

errores_previstos.respuesta: sensate
errores_previstos.explicacion: Sensate is a rare word (“perceiving through the senses”); it does not mean showing good judgement.

errores_previstos.respuesta: sensibly
errores_previstos.explicacion: Sensibly is the adverb; before idea you need the adjective sensible.

glosario.definicion_l: showing reason or sound judgment · able to feel or perceive
something that remunerates

ejercicios.frase: The bus conductor drove too fast on the motorway.
respuestas: The bus driver drove too fast on the motorway.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that conductor is the person who directs an orchestra or a ticket inspector (on a bus or train, the person who sells or checks tickets) and that Spanish “conductor” is driver. The clue is the verb drove: the person who drives is the driver.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The person who drives is the “driver”.
ejercicios.traduccion: El conductor del autobús conducía demasiado rápido por la autopista.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The bus conductor drove too fast on the motorway.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: a conductor is a ticket inspector or the person who directs an orchestra, not the person who drives.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The bus pilot drove too fast on the motorway.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A pilot flies a plane or drives in races; for buses, say driver.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The bus chauffeur drove too fast on the motorway.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A chauffeur is a private driver of a car; the person who drives a bus is a driver.

glosario.definicion_l: the operator of a motor vehicle · someone who drives animals that pull a vehicle
the person who leads a musical group · a substance that readily conducts e.g. electricity and heat
a broad highway designed for high-speed traffic

ejercicios.frase: My grandparents live in the ___, far from any town.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table shows that camp is a place with tents or huts (es: campamento) and that Spanish “campo” (as opposed to the town) is countryside, while field is a specific piece of land for crops or sport. The clue is far from any town: it refers to rural areas in general. The countryside, with the article, is the natural expression (es: vivir en el campo).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “el campo” (as opposed to the town) is “the countryside”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mis abuelos viven en el campo, lejos de cualquier pueblo.

por_opcion.countryside: Correct: the countryside = rural areas (es: el campo).
por_opcion.camp: Incorrect: a camp is a place with tents or huts (summer camp), not rural areas.
por_opcion.field: Incorrect: a field is a specific piece of land (of wheat, a football field); you don't say live in the field to mean living in the countryside.

glosario.definicion_l: rural regions

glosario.significado: campo (terreno concreto, de cultivo o deporte)
glosario.definicion_l: a piece of land cleared of trees and usually enclosed · a region where a battle is being (or has been) fought
providing sophisticated amusement by virtue of having artificially (and vulgarly) mannered or banal or sentimental qualities · temporary living quarters specially built by the army for soldiers

descripcion_larga_es: False friends are English words that look like a Spanish word but mean something else: actually is not Spanish “actualmente”, sensible is not Spanish “sensible”, library is not Spanish “librería”. Because they look alike, Spanish speakers use them without hesitation and do not notice the mistake, but the listener does. Learning each one with its correct equivalent avoids misunderstandings, sometimes funny and sometimes serious, even at advanced levels.

contexto.que_es: They are pairs of words with a similar form in English and Spanish, usually from a common Latin origin, whose meanings have drifted apart over time. Some are complete false friends (embarrassed and Spanish “embarazada” share nothing) and others are partial (argument is a quarrel, but also a logical argument; compromise is an agreement, not an obligation).
contexto.por_que_importa: They are mistakes the speaker cannot see, because the sentence looks correct, and they can completely change the message: saying that someone is embarrassed when you mean pregnant, or that you assisted at a conference instead of attended it. In a professional text or an exam, a false friend damages credibility and can lead to serious misunderstandings.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: They appear in any situation, but above all when translating mentally from Spanish, in learned or technical words that seem transparent (actually, eventually, realise, resume, contest). The warning sign is precisely that an English word looks very like a Spanish one: it is worth checking. For each one, the table on the card gives the English word that matches the Spanish meaning.
